title: Phrase-briefing
goal: Two common words as one stroke: what qualifies, how the stroke is built, which words may lose a stroke to a phrase, limits.

blocks.x: A **phrase entry** is two already-settled words merged into one shorter outline: 2 strokes become 1 for a common pair. Phrase entries are ordinary dictionary entries: strike the chord, get both words. The *phrasing grammar* (one stroke built from pronoun, verb and tense keys) is separate: see [lesson 19](#/lesson/19-phrasing-grammar) and [lesson 20](#/lesson/20-phrasing-strokes).
The idea

[[of|-F]] and [[the|-T]] share no key, not even the star, so their union `-FT` is unused by anything else. That stroke is the phrase [[of the|-FT]]. *of the* is the most frequent word pair in the corpus (2,766,332,391 occurrences).
A phrase stroke is always the **bitwise union of the two words' strokes**, with no join key. Rule: **strike the keys of both words together in one stroke.**
Pressing both words' keys in one stroke differs from pressing them as two strokes, so a phrase stroke is never hit by accident while writing the two words separately.
What qualifies
A word pair (bigram) earns a phrase entry only when **all four** hold:

items: **Both words have a settled primary outline, and at least one is exactly one stroke.** "Primary" is the outline the generator chose (a brief, the plain rules reading, a spelling variant or a star-ladder step). A bonus entry (short form, alternate, backup) never counts, even when cheaper. The other word's primary may be any length.
**The one-stroke word's whole primary and the other word's first stroke share no key**, star included. When both are one stroke: the two primaries are disjoint.

**The merged outline is free, or the pair is worth more than the word that holds it** (see [Phrases compete for strokes](#/ref/phrases/phrases-compete-for-strokes)). A reserved stroke, a suffix, a hand-written `[word]` outline in `rules/briefs.toml` and another phrase are never taken.

**The pair is among the top 20,000 bigrams by raw count** (`PHRASE_TOP_N`). The count is raw, not a collocation score: pairs of two very common function words (*of the*, *in the*) are the ones worth briefing, and a collocation measure ranks them low.

blocks.x: Two eligible pairs on the same outline: the pair said more often in the corpus wins; the phrase text is the final deterministic tie-break.
Primary outlines only

A phrase is built from each word's **primary** outline, never from a bonus entry, even when the word has a cheaper one (backup, short form). A word's own primary never changes because a phrase exists; the "one single-stroke outline per word" rule is untouched.
Exception, competition for a stroke (below): a phrase may take a stroke a word holds as a *short form or alternate*, since the word keeps its primary.
A multi-stroke word in the phrase

When one word (the **filler**) has a one-stroke primary and the other (the **host**) has a primary of any length, the filler's stroke merges into the host's **first stroke only**. Later host strokes carry over unchanged, join keys included.

items: Outline = `[filler OR host's first stroke, host's remaining strokes...]`.
The merged first stroke has no join key, like any first stroke: the phrase starts a new word.
Both orders work: one-stroke word before a multi-stroke word, and multi-stroke word followed by a one-stroke word.
*added by* [[PWAEUD/+-D]]: *added* (two strokes) with *by* merged into its first stroke.

blocks.x: Other multi-stroke examples in the dictionary: `ABD/+-D` *be added*, `ADZ/+-D` *was added*, `AED/+-D` *he added*, `ABGT/+SEU` *the accuracy*, `ABT/+STRAT` *the abstract*.
About 250 phrase entries have more than one stroke; the rest are a single stroke.
The pronoun I

The word list is all lowercase, including the pronoun. The dictionary's *I* is capitalized, *I* [[EU]]; the bare letter is fingerspelled. A bigram containing *i* is looked up as *I*, and its phrase is written capitalized: *I would* [[WOEU]], not "i would". Same for *I'm*, *I'd*, *I've*, *I'll*. Most pairs starting with *I* get no phrase entry: [[EU]] shares its vowel keys with almost every verb.
Phrases compete for strokes
A pair whose merged stroke a word already holds can take it. `it is` is `T` + `S` = [[ST]]; it displaced a backup of *sit*. The pair takes the stroke when
pair count / all pairs x 25 000  >  word count / all words x (cost of its next-best outline - cost of the stolen one)

Left side: one stroke saved (a phrase has its two words' keys and one stroke fewer; a stroke weighs 25 keys, see [How short](#/ref/brevity)). Right side: what the word loses by moving. Pair counts: `bigrams_en.txt`; word counts: the subtitle frequency list.
What a phrase can never take

items: A reserved stroke, a suffix stroke, a hand-written `[word]` outline in `briefs.toml`, another phrase.
An entry settled by the star ladder, or a family-shaped entry (a family member is defined by its stem).
A **backup** (a stem plus an ending you already know): losing one costs the word nothing under the rule above, but backups are the predictable multi-stroke way in.
The **primary of a stem** (a word other words are built from). *object* keeps [[OBT]], so *on the* does not get it.

blocks.x: Protected words and the takeover limit

items: **The 5,000 most frequent words keep their primary** (`PROTECTED_WORDS`). [[on|OB]], [[want|W-T]] and [[after|AF]] stay. A phrase may still take a *short form* or *alternate* from them.

**Only the 1,000 most frequent eligible pairs may take a held stroke** (`TAKEOVER_TOP_N`). A rarer pair goes only into a free stroke. Without this limit, 373 words ended up with a star because a pair nobody will learn had taken their plain stroke.

**A word that loses its only way of being written gets another**: its next-best outline, or its best own candidate of any length that nobody holds. *antonio* moves to `TPHOEPBT`. A pair is skipped if the word would end up with nothing. A word that loses its primary is no longer part of any later phrase.
A word in a committed phrase is not taken from afterwards.

blocks.x: Size of the result

Current build: 7,373 phrase entries, 5,207 merges and the rest borrowed (next section). 89 phrases took a stroke from a rarer word. A merge joins two strokes you know into one: *in the* is the stroke for *in* plus the stroke for *the*.
Phrases borrowed from other dictionaries

Plover, Lapwing and the fifteen other theories ([other theories' briefs](#/ref/collisions)) also write two-word phrases as one stroke: `O*T` *to the*, `TKW-PBLT` *do not*. Some pairs cannot merge (shared key) or merge onto a stroke a word holds. For those the pass offers the dictionaries' one-stroke phrases, in the same arbitration as a merge, ranked by pair frequency. Rules:

items: **The merge comes first.** If the pair merges and the stroke is free (or a word gives it up), the pair is the merge. A borrowed outline is a fallback, tried cheapest first; a pair is committed once.

**A borrowed phrase never competes with a merge for a stroke.** If any pair's own merge produces that stroke, the borrowed outline is dropped. Two theories write `ST` for *is the*, said more often than *it is*, but *it is* is [[ST]] because it is `T` plus `S`.
**Same takeover limits.** A borrowed pair takes a stroke from a word only among the 1,000 commonest candidates, never from a top-5,000 word's primary, and only when worth more than the word loses.
**Only one-stroke, typable outlines of two plain lowercase words.** A phrase with a number or a capital is skipped, as is anything on a key lyk does not have.

blocks.x: Effect: phrases 5,207 to 7,373, comfort per word 92.8 to 92.6, every other guard and the solver numbers unchanged. [[to the|TOTD]], [[on the|O*LT]] and [[to be|TORB]] have one-stroke phrases. A borrowed phrase must be memorized; a merge can be worked out, hence the merge first.
Not covered

items: **Both words multi-stroke.** At least one side must be a one-stroke filler.
**Three or more words.** No chaining of phrases (unlike backups, which chain: *green* + *house* = *greenhouse*, then + `+-Z`).
**A backup or short form as a component.** Only primaries are used.
**Removing a join-key boundary inside an existing multi-stroke word.** A different mechanism.

blocks.x: Where it runs

One pass, run once after the backup pass settles and before the "stranded" diagnostic is computed; it sees the final dictionary, backups included. Phrase entries have their own origin (`Phrase`); the stroke read-back never treats a phrase as a word: a continuation stroke after `-FT` is not read as *of the* plus an ending. See [the stroke read-back](#/ref/fallback).
What it saves

The quote benchmark walks a passage left to right, taking a phrase entry whenever one covers the next two words. Phrases save **strokes**, not keys: a phrase's key count is exactly the sum of its two words' key counts; the stroke count drops by one per hit. A phrase is built from primaries while a word may be credited with a cheaper backup, so the phrase-aware walk can occasionally spend a few more keys than word-by-word, always with fewer strokes.
Quote benchmark, all limits above: the phrase-aware walk uses 1,092 strokes on the 103 hand-picked passages and 5,756 on the 416 extracted ones: about 12% and 9% fewer than word by word.
A bigram limit of 40,000 would save about 1.6% more strokes but add around 13,500 phrases to learn; rejected.
